chunks: Advantages of an OS over bare-metal. The question: What advantages does it have over bare-metal?
An OS gives structure and predictable timing as a system grows. Each activity becomes its own task, written as simple code that can wait.
The scheduler runs the most urgent task first. You also get ready-made tools such as queues, locks and network stacks.
The price is some RAM for each task, a little CPU time, and new kinds of bugs.
Think of a hospital emergency room. The nurses always take the most urgent patient first, so a new routine check-up does not delay a heart attack.
A plain loop is more like a single line where everyone is served in order, so each new routine patient makes the urgent one wait longer. The OS is the triage system.
It costs some staff time, but urgent cases stay urgent.
The super-loop's latency climbs one-for-one with every millisecond of background work and is already above the 1 milliseconds deadline at x = 0 (15.
5 milliseconds), while the RTOS line stays near 0. 017 milliseconds.
In a bare-metal design you fix this with ISRs and chopped state machines; in an RTOS you get it from the priority.
Task: one activity the OS runs, with its own stack of working memory. Priority: a number saying how urgent a task is.
Preemption: pausing a running task so a more urgent one can run at once. Semaphore / queue: ready-made ways for tasks to signal each other or pass data safely.
Middleware: ready-made software such as a network stack or file system that builds on an OS.
A device has a control job that must run every 1 milliseconds. With a simple main loop, you add a feature that takes 40 milliseconds.
Now the control job can wait 40 milliseconds or more in the loop, and its 1 milliseconds deadline is broken.
With an RTOS (a small real-time OS), you add the feature as a low-priority task. The control task preempts it and still runs within microseconds of becoming ready.
The cost is a stack for each task plus a percent or two of CPU for the tick. That is the whole idea.
"The advantages are structure and predictable timing.

Each activity becomes a task that can block on events, and priority preemption bounds the latency of urgent work regardless of how much other work exists, while a super-loop's latency grows with every feature.
You also get tested mutexes, queues and timers, reusable middleware like TCP/IP and USB, portability and cleaner team boundaries.
The costs are RAM for stacks, a percent or two of CPU, and concurrency bugs."
